idiom_name: start method returning immediately + exactly-once completion event/callback marshalled to the caller's context
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: a start method validates its arguments, allocates a per-call operation record (result slot, cancellation flag, caller state) and schedules the work on the host's background mechanism, then returns. The operation runs off the caller's context, optionally posts progress notifications, and on every exit path - success, failure or cancellation - delivers exactly one completion notification through the host's dispatcher, which marshals it back to the context that started the call. The caller registers a handler (or awaits the notification), distinguishes the three outcomes from the payload, and uses the per-call state token to identify which invocation completed when several are outstanding. Where the language has a composable awaitable abstraction, encode the same phases with it and keep the event form for multi-consumer streams; the classic structure stays justified when the host owns the event loop or a foreign API offers only a completion callback.
pitfalls: Raising the completion on the worker's thread instead of the caller's context, so every consumer becomes a synchronisation problem.
Skipping the completion on some path (exception, cancellation, early return): callers wait forever and the bug only appears on the failing path.
Reusing one operation record for concurrent invocations, so completions can no longer be attributed to their requests.

Pyramid of doom / callback hell: nesting multiple asynchronous calls where each registers its own completion handler inside the previous — deeply indented, hard to follow error paths and impossible to extract into reusable units. Solved by promises, async/await or continuation-chaining.

async void fire-and-forget (especially in C# / JavaScript): async methods returning void instead of Task propagate exceptions to the synchronisation context and crash the process unobserved. Reserve async void only for genuine top-level event handlers; make all library surfaces return Task or Promise.

Wrong delivery order (emit before register): raising a completion event on a subject before any listener has subscribed — the caller misses it and waits indefinitely. Detectable with pre-subscription state checks or by switching to a deferred/buffered subject.

Reactor vs Proactor confusion: using a synchronous-readiness-demultiplexing pattern (Reactor) for an inherently asynchronous I/O model, or vice versa — leads to either blocking threads or missing completion notifications. Choose based on whether the underlying I/O is synchronous (select/poll) or asynchronous (completion ports, kernel AIO, libuv).

Event-channel flooding: a progress or data event channel that fires hundreds of times per second overwhelms the dispatcher's queue and causes UI jank or handler starvation. Throttle, debounce or batch progress events before posting them.

Silent drop on the exception path: raising completion with error=null or success=true on a path that also logs/throws an exception — the caller receives success but the error is lost. Ensure completion carries the error and is the sole notification channel on every exit path.

Wrong move: subscribe a fresh per-operation handler on a long-lived emitter and never unsubscribe -> the emitter retains every subscriber (Node prints MaxListenersExceededWarning past the default 10 listeners; a C# event's publisher strong reference keeps even disposed subscribers alive) and re-runs stale handlers -> instead unsubscribe with once()/off() on every path including errors, or bridge the event into a single-shot promise/TaskCompletionSource.

Wrong move: start a second operation on a single-invocation component while one is in flight -> the component throws InvalidOperationException or overwrites the in-flight operation record, so the first caller's completion is lost or misattributed -> instead use the multiple-invocation userState overload, or serialize starts behind an explicit busy check.

Wrong move: block the caller's own context waiting for the completion event (sleep-poll a flag, .Result on a bridged task) -> the completion is queued to the very context now blocked and the operation deadlocks -> instead register the handler and return control to the loop, or await the TaskCompletionSource-wrapped bridge without ever blocking that context.
